utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Could we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. My name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues, Ms. McHenry, Mr. Turone and Ms. Udo for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. My name is Edina Residovic, Defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic, along with my colleague, Eugene O'Sullivan, professor from Canada

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. My name is Zeljko Olujic, representing the defence for Mr. Zdravko Mucic, along with my colleague Mr. Michael Greaves. The Defence has a request. Could Mr. Mucic be examined by a physician on Monday. He has several health problems, including spine problems, stomach problems and certain mental problems that arose in the last 48 hours, so we would like to request that Mr. Mucic be allowed to see a doctor on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo, Defence counsel for Mr. Hazim Delic, along with Mr. Thomas Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Cynthia McMurrey and, along with Ms. Nancy Boler, we represent Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. With regard to Mr. Olujic's application, I am sure Mr. Mucic knows that there are no obstacles to him seeing a doctor while he is in the prison there. There is sufficient provision made for him to see doctors if he has any problems. That should not be a problem at all, to see the doctors -- the Victims and Witness Unit is there to liaise and make sure that he sees who ever he thinks might be is necessary to assist him. I do not see any problem with that at all. I think it might be more appropriate, if he prefers Tuesday, for a proper examination, which is a holiday, and Wednesday is also a free day here, because we will not be sitting, so he has two full days within which he can get his arrangements made.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: We take note of that, your Honours. However, I do not know at this point what is the nature of his health problems, what is his mental state, what is his physical condition. He is suffering from different varieties of pain and he also is not very focused. It all speaks to the fact that his overall condition has been deteriorating. I do not know when he is going to be able to see the physicians, but we take note of your decision and we will try to comply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any time he wants to, he should consult those at the prison so he can see a doctor. Do you have any applications to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just a short matter. Nothing in relation to that -- I thought that matter was resolved. Just, your Honour, that we filed a motion to exclude Defence documents, and I think, basically we have resolved those issues which we envisaged would arise as a consequence of that motion, so we withdraw it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we have the witness? Mr. Moran, do you have anything to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: We filed a response to that motion and given the fact that the issues are resolved and the motion is withdrawn, the response is withdrawn along with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed. Thank you -- remind the witness he is still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, Sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand. MUHAMED VEJZAGIC (continued)

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have you rested from the efforts of yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So, so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we move on to the next area of questioning, I would like the volume III of the files to be given to the witness as well as volume I, because it is in volume I that the expert report of the Brigadier is contained. Brigadier, you recall that at the end of the hearing yesterday we talked about Tactical Groups; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please find the annex VI/3, there is a chart there and I want to ask you questions regarding this chart. It is in volume III of the file: have you found it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is this the chart of the Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to remind you again that we are not trying to confirm either the authenticity or truthfulness of the chart. We would just like to touch on certain issues relating to the Tactical Group. Brigadier, yesterday, you explained that the black fields signify the soldiers that are subordinated to the Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You see in this chart there is a rubric which says "TO Konjic"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The black rubric there, would it also represent soldiers that would be subordinated to the Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, what is in black are the Konjic units that were part of the Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: These soldiers from Konjic, who were subordinated to the Tactical Group, under whose command were they at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All parts from all these municipalities that were part of the Tactical Group were directly subordinated to the commander of the Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The white areas, according to this chart, would represent the military that is not subordinated to the Tactical Group. Could you please tell me, under whose command would the soldiers who were not part of the Tactical Group be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, I cannot hear the interpreter, so I do not know when to start. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you may. Did you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The soldiers who were not subordinated to the Tactical Group, under whose command would they remain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The soldiers who are represented in white would be under the command of the municipal headquarters and they would be subordinated to the commander of that TO, so, apart from these 300 soldiers who were part of the Tactical Group, the remainder of them would be under the command of the commander of the TO.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, provided that the information in this chart is true, out of these 2,000 soldiers that Konjic had, to whom would the 1700 soldiers who were not subordinated to the Tactical Group be so subordinated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These soldiers would remain under the municipal staff -- they would not be included in tactical groups and this is clear from this graph -- those 300 soldiers, which were represented in black colour, would be a part of the Tactical Group and their commander is a commander of the Tactical Group as well as everybody else who is part of this Tactical Group, whereas this remaining 1700 soldiers keep their positions on the front-lines and they are under the command of the commander of the TO.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, do you recall yesterday, when explaining the reasons for the establishment of Tactical Groups for the lifting of the siege of Sarajevo, that you said that certain forces from certain areas were going to be reinforced. So my question to you now is: these forces, regardless of the Tactical Groups, existed in the municipal headquarters of the Territorial Defence -- to whom were they subordinated before the Tactical Groups were established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is normal that these units would be under the command of the municipal headquarters before they came absorbed into the Tactical Groups.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This plan of the main headquarters, which at that time was still the main staff of the Territorial Defence, to reinforce certain forces, did it mean that all these units from the -- that all units that belonged to the Territorial Defence would be absorbed into Tactical Groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that does not imply that, even though there was a plan to reinforce certain forces in order to lift the siege of Sarajevo, because you cannot pull all the forces from the front-lines, where they were holding positions before the Tactical Groups were established. So part of the forces remained in their positions, because, in a way, these municipalities are threatened at all times and if they left their positions, the enemy could take control over those positions and could threaten the towns that they were defending.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, is my understanding of what you testified to yesterday and what you just said now that the reinforcing was made in such a way that only parts of the units of the Territorial Defence forces were used in order to establish Tactical Groups -- was that my proper understanding of what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is a proper understanding of what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Brigadier. In your supporting material, which you provided, with your report, there is an order of 27 July 1992, by which Zejnil Delalic was appointed commander of, as it says, "All forces", so will you please find that document -- it is your annex 6 through 5.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, based on your personal and professional experience, can you tell us, is it necessary for the commander of Tactical Group to receive precise orders as to which units and what equipment is being subordinated to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In any event, when a superior person is tasking a subordinate, he has to be as precise as possible -- as accurate as possible and not place the subordinate into any doubt as to what the order actually contains, so each order has to be clear and accurate so that the subordinate can understand it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, according to your overall professional knowledge, does the Tactical Group have authority over the entire area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said yesterday that the concept of the Tactical Group implies a temporary or provisional formation and a limited task, which is either in a particular area, or within the general area, so the commander of the Tactical Group does not have an overall superiority -- he only has authority over those units that have become part of this Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, yesterday you talked to us about the district headquarters. Where they existed, is it true that these district staffs were superior bodies to the municipal staffs in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is very accurately spelt out in law. That means that the district staff is subordinated to the chief staff -- the main staff -- and the municipal staffs are subordinated to the district staffs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, you were also very precise when you said to whom the municipal staffs were subordinated where there were no district staffs. However, I am going to ask you whether, both in theory and practice of our army, a Tactical Group had competencies of a district staff at any time under any circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we should not confuse concepts here. The concept of district staff and of Tactical Groups are two very different concepts. The district staff has authority over all forces in his area, whereas the Tactical Group does not and I think I said that very clearly. It is a provisional formation tasked with a particular task and that means it has to solve certain problems, that means to take a certain area, and it is time limited as well. As soon as the need for its activity is finished, the Tactical Group may be resolved -- the commander may retain -- if there is enough need -- if it is to be used in the future in combat operations, he can retain certain forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So far, Brigadier, we have not talked about corps. Tell me, since we talked about this during the examination of the Prosecution witnesses, in theory and practice of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did the Tactical Group have, at any time, authorities of a corps or competencies of a corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that from everything I have so far stated, it is clear that the Tactical Group may not be a basis for a formation of a corps. I keep repeating that this is a provisional formation and corps cannot come out of or issue out of Tactical Groups. They can be established from other units that had already been established into brigades, and only by combining these forces, that is, brigades and divisions, corps can be formed. So, there are certain formations that make a corps, so brigades and divisions make the corps but not Tactical Groups, because they are provisional formations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I believe, Brigadier, that you have answered my question, but, in order to make sure that we have complete clarity, I am going to repeat part of the question. So, in the military theory and practice of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, were Tactical Groups which were formed in order to lift the siege of Sarajevo -- did they ever have competencies of a corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All Tactical Groups, which were established as provisional formations, had particular tasks. They had no further tasks, or they were never the basis for the formation of corps. Again, I repeat, a Tactical Group is there to complete or to carry out a task. Once the task is carried out, they pull out, they dissolve, so this cannot be a base -- a Tactical Group cannot be a basis for a formation of a brigade or let alone a corps, so I think it is superfluous for me to go on explaining this. There is no question that this was used as a basis for a formation of a corps, if I understood you correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Brigadier, you also talked about the law on armed forces and other regulations, which regulated the issues of the army and its development. In these regulations, are there any provisions for a formation or duty that would be called a commander of all forces -- of all formations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the regulations used in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there is no such title like a "commander of all forces". That is not clear. "Commander of all forces" means nothing. There are commanders who have certain formations -- certain units, so that is a commander of a battalion. It is clear what it is. He has 500 soldiers, and then also there is a commander of a brigade and so on and so forth. There are such titles, there are such formations, and those are commanders of such units and a "commander of all forces" is a rather vague term.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, could you please now look at the appointment of the 27 July 1992 and you put it in the section on Tactical Group. So, based on this document and other documents that Zejnil Delalic, as a commander of a Tactical Group in this period, issued, how do you interpret this appointment? Is this an appointment of a commander of a Tactical Group, or, to be more precise, did this appointment change his title of the commander of Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the basis of the contents of this appointment, the only thing that is clear is that the area of operation was widened. However, he is still the commander of Tactical Group, and interpretation of all formations is without a basis, because in the area where his appointment as a commander of Tactical Group is concerned, there are other formations -- there is HVO, there are MUP forces, so the HVO forces were at no time subordinated to the staff of the supreme command and then, as well, neither did MUP, so they each had their own chain of commands. So, such an appointment could not have been implemented. It is completely vague -- this should have been spelt out much clearer, or issued a new order as to which forces, what materiel, which equipment were part of this Tactical Group, what its task was. Maybe there are such documents, but I did not see them. However, this is completely insufficient, it is too vague, and it is not implementable.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You answered this question yesterday, but, for purposes of continuity, I am going to ask you once again so that we can hear your answer once again. You said yesterday that one Tactical Group was formed in mid May. Who was its first commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first commander of Tactical Group number 1 was Mr. Mustafa Polutak.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who was the chief of staff of Tactical Group of number 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The chief of staff of Tactical Group 1 was Sucuro Pilica from the beginning of its formation to the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said from "beginning to end". Was Sucuro Pilica the chief of staff of TG1 when the commander of TG1 was Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where was the commanding positions of Tactical Group 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pazaric, which is about 30 kilometres away from Sarajevo. During the combat operations, it had to be -- the position had to be changed, depending on the fighting, because the commander has to change his positions, depending on the course of the fighting itself. Maybe the headquarters remained in Pazaric, maybe it was moved later on to other places, where the major force was situated, so the commander had to follow the fighting, the combat, and move his troops around accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, you said that several Tactical Groups were formed and yesterday you spoke about Tactical Group 1 and Tactical Group Visoko. What other Tactical Group was formed with the task of taking part in lifting the siege of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In mid July, Tactical Group number 2 was set up.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what direction of activity this Tactical Group number 2 was entrusted with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tactical Group number 2 was in the region of Mount Igman and oriented its activities towards the field of Sarajevo in four directions -- one direction was towards Igman-Trnovo-Igman; the second was towards Kula; the third was towards Krupac-Kjeste-Tjenje, towards Svenje-Klanac, and one towards the source of Bosna. So those were the four directions under the jurisdiction of Tactical Group number 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, from which compositions of the municipal forces did they recruit, or were soldiers subordinated to for Tactical Group number 2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tactical Group number 2 was much stronger in terms of equipment and manpower. It had over 5,000 men, it had an artillery division, it had 25 weapons, it had three tanks, it had about 5,000 men, as I say, from the Ilidza-Trnovo-Hadzic region, so from this area, which gravitates around Mount Igman.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, according to what you have said, Tactical Group 2 subordinated part of the forces from the Hadzic municipality, that is to say, Pazarici and Tarcin and Hrasnica - Ilidza or Hrasnica, from which part of the forces were subordinated to Tactical Group 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me, please, in view of the appointment we spoke about a moment ago, we see the direction towards which part of the forces were subordinated to in terms of Tactical Group number 1. Can you tell me, who were -- to whom were the municipal staff of Prozor subordinated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I understood your question correctly, regardless of the fact that the forces from Prozor took part in this operation, the command -- the municipal headquarters were always linked to the district headquarters of Zenica, whereas the municipal headquarters of Zenica were always linked to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The municipal headquarters of Jablanica and Konjic, where there was no district headquarters, to whom were they subordinated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As the district headquarters of Mostar was not in function, they were directly linked -- they were directly under the command of the supreme command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, can you tell us whether this state of affairs existed up until the formation of the corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was the situation right up until the formation of the army -- for the given territories, when all the forces in those areas were pulled together, there was an enlargement, a reinforcement of forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Under the command of which corps did the compositions of the forces coming from the Jablanica and Konjic area come, once the corps had been formed -- who were they subordinate to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The forces of the municipal headquarters of Konjic and Jablanica became part of the 4th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The composition of which corps encompassed the forces which were to be found in the municipality of Hadzici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hadzici were always within the composition of the Sarajevo region and during the war they belonged to the Corps I. Once the district headquarters were abolished, these forces were incorporated in to the Corps I.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, I have asked you several questions linked to the formation of TG2 and the formation of the corps: in view of your functions during the war in the staff of the supreme command, is the knowledge and your appraisals and your personal knowledge stated before this court -- did you fulfil your duties within the main headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I took part in all these events because I was a member of the chief of staff of the supreme command, and I can say full well that that was how things stood.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your documents and your expert report, you spoke of the formation and Operation South. Can you tell us something about that Operation? I should like to ask you to look at annex VI/9? In fact, it is VI/8 and VI/9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, whether the supreme command at a given time, in order to try and lift the siege of Sarajevo, did it bring in the decision about Operation South?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As the problem of deblocking Sarajevo was one that was present all the time, the State and military leadership sought ways of dealing with this problem -- of lifting the siege of Sarajevo, and, within the context of that problem, we have a decision on the provisional organisation and formation of the units of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, please, were you convinced that this decision existed in the archives of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the decision it can be seen that a provisional command was set up and a decree was passed by which the headquarters would be on Mount Igman. Furthermore, from point 2, we see the composition of the units and of the command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, were there appointments for the provisional command of Operation South? Would you look at document VI/9 -- are you convinced that this document exists in the archives of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether this provisional command for the South Group, in its composition, gave certain functions, appointments to Mr. Zejnil Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes -- under item 3.3, you will find the name of Mr. Zejnil Delalic as an assistant commander, deputy commander, for logistics.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, does the commander of a formation such as a Tactical Group, for example, can he, in keeping with military rules and regulations, and your professional knowledge in that matter, can the commander of a formation, in addition to the competencies that he has in that particular formation, can he, from his superior officers or superior command, be given an additional special task?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe I said yesterday that this is a different principle -- that another principle testifies to the fact that a subordinate must unconditionally carry out the orders of his superiors, whether those superiors are individuals or are the commands, so every order received by a superior must be carried out by a subordinate unless the order would embody a criminal act, which means that he can be given different orders and he is duty bound to carry them out in addition to his regular duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, can you tell me, please, whether Mr. Delalic, as the commander of Tactical Group number 1, after his appointment -- his nomination -- did he have duties to perform as assistant commander for the logistics group for the whole of the Jug South operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic's appointment to the provisional group of the command of the south did not mean that he ceased to perform his duties as the commander of Tactical Group number 1, so he remained responsible for this unit under his command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, does your research show that, within the frameworks of the south, the Jug operation, the forces of Tactical Group number 1 were in their previous composition, or were they reinforced and what was their direction of activity? Were you able to draw any conclusions along those lines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tactical Group 1, which took part in Operation South -- Jug -- for this particular task was reinforced by about 2,000 men from the Fojnica municipality. The direction of its activities was Pazaric and then towards Malo Polje -- that was one direction -- towards Igman -- that is the first direction; the second was from Ormanja across Kocan -- I cannot quite remember, but two directions of activity towards Kocan, but for the most part TG1, the direction was towards Hadzici and towards Igman, the village of Lokve, that is the general direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was the bulk of the force in that operation located along some other direction, and if so which was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to military theory and practice, we have the main force and the auxiliary force. We know that the main force is there to perform the main attack -- the major attack, whereas the auxiliary forces, which are weaker, are backup forces, and if we said that the forces of TG2 were stronger and that they had over 5,000 men, then they were the protagonists of the combat operations towards lifting the siege of Sarajevo, whereas the forces of Tactical Group 1 were in an auxiliary direction and had the task of communication, to link these Serb forces which defended themselves along Hadzici and up by Brezovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, tell me, please, whether this area of Igman, Hadzic, Pazarici was the first liberated free area outside the ring around of the blockade around Sarajevo, with the exception of Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, if you look at what the free space -- this free area was at the time, one of our brigades was in Hrasnica and it kept this free area towards Igman. There were good conditions for the defence there. Part of the other brigade was in Dobrinja -- those were the 4th and 5th Brigades, whereas the area -- by clearing up Bradina and Donje Selo we had an area stretching from Jablanica across Tarcin, Pazarici right up to Igman and this was a free area -- it was a sort of channel, canal by which we could communicate with the encirclement around Sarajevo. Hadzici were under the Serb side and this pass -- you were not able to communicate. You had to go across the hills via the village of Lokve across the hills of Igman to Sarajevo and this was -- came to be known as the "road of salvation", because it was the only way to reach Sarajevo and to get supplies and other necessary equipment to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, in view of the fact that this court is very well acquainted with the situation regarding Sarajevo, how difficult the communications were for everyone, especially for the organs of power and authority and the military organs with other parts of the territory, and how far these were conditioned by the lack of telephone communications, the lack of gas, satellite communications which were severed frequently and so on, my question is the following: did the supreme command use the commanders who were located on the first lines behind the blockade of the city sometimes to convey information and orders or anything else towards the other commands -- the other headquarters within the republic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, in Sarajevo, we only had two or three satellite links -- one in the presidency, but there were no satellite links with the units themselves. Second, are you asking me whether the links functioned, whether they were working, operative? No -- everything was destroyed during the war and we used radio communication mostly, short-range radio communication, openly without any crypto-protection, so that if you tuned into that particular wave length, you would be able to hear what was going on. You could even give different commands and use disinformation and we did have cases of disinformation in this way, in the area of the Corps IV, the enemy would give contrary orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, in view of this overall situation which you have described, were there occasions when the commanders, commandeers of Hadzici, TG1 and so on and so forth sometimes used -- conveyed orders which a courier would bring with him. Did this occur in practice, did the commanders and other military personnel at times, were they used to convey orders from the supreme command towards other compositions, other headquarters, did this ever occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this practice did take place frequently in other parts of the battlefield as well, because, if you did not have a radio station -- a long-range radio station and a message was sent to somebody who was far away, then it had to be relayed by the commanders from their superiors downwards -- it was a sort of transmission, a relay.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, we discussed Operation South -- Jug. Tell us, please, whether this was one of the large-scale attempts to lift the siege of Sarajevo in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, according to the composition of the forces, in the course of the war, we never had such a large formation, because we know why this was done -- there were 7,000 men there, in those conditions a lot of artillery was at their disposal and this composition had the force of an operative group, but the signatories, along with this provisional composition, because it was a provisional composition, could have been called an operative group by virtue of its size and by virtue of its title -- Jug, South. When an operation is formed, it is given a code name, and the code name for this operation was Operation South. There was Vihor or Oluja as the Croats had, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, do you know how long Operation South lasted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Operation South was prepared minutely -- it took some time to equip the men with material, to see to supplies, logistic problems -- it is no simple matter to set up as much manpower and equipment as is necessary for combat, and this lasted all through August -- it started on 17, I think -- around about the 17th, and went on until 22 September, if I recall correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Brigadier, I would like to ask you now to take a look at annex under V-C/11?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What was the number again?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: C/11. Do you have it as an order, in fact a document of 24 August 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You just said that a superior command could task a particular commander or soldier with whatever task. Could you please look at the document you have enclosed in your file and tell me if this is one of the documents that you relied upon when you formed your opinion -- is this a special task issued to a commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can say the following on the basis of this document. The commander of the facility was directly subordinated to the supreme command and in that capacity he asked his superior, in this case the supreme command, and he asked for assistance, because this facility could potentially be threatened, which meant that certain forces, whether military or paramilitary, may try to take this facility, since a large part of the forces were out on the front-lines, a number of forces were incorporated in the Tactical Group, so he is asking for assistance. This document is addressed to Delalic, because, at that period, the supreme command staff probably could not resolve this problem -- I think this person's name was Zerif Grabavica -- he was the commander of this facility and so he asked to get in touch with this person to try and resolve the problem. He is passing on or transmitting a message to a commander on the ground and is telling him to get in touch with this person and to try to resolve this problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So, this is a special task which is not part of his duty as a commander of Tactical Group, is that a correct understanding of what you just said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a subsequent task, because it has nothing to do with his command of particular units, but it is to provide assistance to someone who is directly subordinated to the supreme command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, can we just -- can we look at the annex, the attachment you have, marked with V-D/41. Is this document of Tactical Group 1 of 24 August 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, based on everything you have testified to so far, can you tell us whether these are the original duties of the commander of Tactical Group 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain this a bit further?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the preamble, you can see that the commander of the Tactical Group received this order from the superior command, because it says, "Pursuant to the order of the supreme command of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina" and so on and so forth -- he is turning to the municipal headquarters of Konjic, and telling them what tasks are to be taken by the headquarters in Konjic, so in the preamble he is referring to the order of the supreme command headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, based on your overall professional experience, would this document be part of the basis on which you formed your opinion as to what it means to receive a special order or a task of transmission from a superior command to a subordinate command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Obviously, we have a transmission here. The supreme command headquarters had no possibility to resolve this in any other way, so they are using the commander of the Tactical Group and you see the date, 24 August. So, by this order, it tasks the commander of the Tactical Group, and I believe this is because of the lack of communications -- he is tasking him to try to resolve the problems listed here with the municipal staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, without this document, that is the provision which you pointed to in the preamble, would a commander of the Tactical Group, given his scope of authority as a commander of a Tactical Group, would he have been able to issue such an order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not at all. I repeat: the commander of the Tactical Group has an exclusive authority over his own formations, that is, the Tactical Group, and he is responsible for everything that happens within this Tactical Group. He had no authority to issue such an order to the commander of the municipal staff, because that is not within his competence, but, as I said, this headquarters, as well as the headquarters in Jablanica, were all directly subordinated to the supreme command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, while we are still at the Tactical Group, does the commander of a Tactical Group have authority, that is, is he in a superior position to the institutions in his area, that is hospitals, schools and such?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In an area where there are certain institutions that have a logistical role in the operations and these can be different institutions, this could be warehouses, factories, prisons -- we all call them in military terms "institutions" -- they are in a certain territory and they have their own management. Again, I repeat: the commander of a Tactical Group is responsible for his own units. He has no competence over these institutions. They have their own directors or managers.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Brigadier, earlier on you said that your research has shown that some time in April 1992, the facility of the former JNA in Celebici, the Celebici barracks was taken over by the legal authorities. Do you know, from your research, whether this military facility in 1992 also housed a prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to the documents and through my research of this issue, I did not find information that Celebici was foreseen as a prison. These were depots and it was a fuel depot. It is first mentioned as a prison in the middle of May, after the prison in Konjic was shelled, and I think it housed about 10 prisoners, and because of the danger from shelling, it was moved to this facility, where it was safe from the shelling by the Serb forces, so that I believe that it was only in mid May that it was first mentioned or used that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, during your research, you also visited the Celebici barracks. Can you please tell us where these barracks are and how big a facility is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The barracks are located in the village of Celebici. It is south, south-west of Konjic along the M17 highway. I think it is set back about 50 or 60 metres. It is visible from the road and it was used as a military facility first, as a fuel depot and a depot for some other materiel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did your research and review of various documents to which you had access, which you mentioned in the beginning of your testimony, serve as a basis for your stating here who were the persons who were detained in the prison which was set up in a part of the Celebici barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first persons were those who were transferred there from the military prison in Konjic, due to shelling. And, later, based on the information that I have, persons who were arrested in Donje Selo and Bradina and Brdjani and other villages where the Serbs offered resistance were brought there. These were, for the most part, persons who were armed and who resisted the legal army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, with your expert report, you also enclosed various annexes -- VII/2, B/2 et cetera, et cetera. The documents which you provided with your report, did it form the basis for your conclusion as to why these persons were brought to this prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In passing yesterday, I said that some armed Serbian people -- I do not want to call them Chetniks -- near Ostrozac, they surrendered their weapons, they received certificates, and, in those certificates it explicitly states that these weapons are temporarily taken from them and they suffered no consequences even though they had illegal weapons. However, those who took part in fighting, they, for the most part, were armed. According to the research -- and we can see that from the statements, some had thrown away their weapons, some say they did not fight, but they were in those positions. So, they were arrested or taken prisoner in locations where there was fighting, there was shooting, where the soldiers of the army were also being killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My question is only why they were brought there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were brought there because they possessed weapons and because they resisted. They fought against the regular army, which, at that time, was looking for a way to lift the siege of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, I do not know if you know this, whether this is within the area of your expertise, but do you know, according to our regulations, who were the competent authorities for detention of persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to the regulations, the bodies of the Ministry of the Interior were the ones who were competent for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, since this is the time that we usually use for a break, and I am about to move on to another area of questioning, would this be a good moment to take a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will now have a break and reassemble at 12 noon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please invite the witness to return to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Brigadier, before the break, we discussed the organs who, according to our regulations, are in charge of detaining and taking individuals prisoner if they are suspected of having committed a crime. You said that this was the task of the Ministry of Internal Affairs. Could you tell us, please, whether, in the former Yugoslav Army there was the military police -- did the military police exist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. According to the regulations of the former Yugoslav People's Army, there was a professional police corps, professional police, which had the task of detaining military personnel in cases where they had committed crimes or violated discipline, or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, in the previous period, that is to say, before the war, and at the beginning of the war, according to the regulations that prevailed, did Territorial Defence have a military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to the existing regulations, this structure of the armed forces did not have a military police, and in case its members during a training exercise in peacetime or wartime had committed violations, or criminal acts, such individuals were the problem of the army police -- came under the competency of the army police. They were sent to army prisons, or civilian prisons, which existed on the territory of a given municipality. So, the Territorial Defence did not have its own prisons or its own police.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your research for your expert report, did you find that, in 1992, after the beginning of the war, the Croatian Defence Council, did it have its own military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my research shows that the HVO forces did have a military police corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does your research provide you with facts and figures, that is, information within the HVO forces at the time, that is to say at the beginning of 1992 -- after the initial war operations, were there members of the Muslim ethnicity -- Bosnians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, among the ranks of the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council, there were quite a significant number of Bosnians. In part, they took part on the battlefield in Bosnia-Herzegovina. There were members of the Muslim nation, and they were within the units of the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Brigadier, may we now take a look at one of the documents that you have in your dossier -- it is document V-D/42?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You said number 42?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is a document of Tactical Group 1 dating back to 28 August 1992. Do you have the same document before you? V-D/42?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The number is 02/349-59 [sic].

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, in view of the explanations you have given us previously, and your expert opinions given, referring to the 24th, I now ask you whether this is also the type of document, the type of order from the commander of the Tactical Group, which is not a component part of his competencies, of his authorisations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From this document, we are able to conclude, according to what the signatory, Mr. Delalic refers to, he refers to a document by the supreme command, which states that, on the basis of the supreme command headquarters, the armed forces number such and such, he is asking for the solution of a particular problem. So, he is not alone -- it was not only the commander of the Tactical Group; it was an order from a superior command, which was the supreme command in this case, and they refer to a particular number, a protocol number, of the document of the particular order to solve the problems that are stipulated under points 1, 2, 3 and 4 and that these problems should be solved.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just a minute. There is a slight error in getting the number of the document -- it is not -59 -- it is -58 -- 02-349-58, not -59?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is -58, it is -58, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Brigadier, may we now look at the document which you have numbered V-D/43, and IV-D/44 -- it is D/44?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that document exists.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, Brigadier, become convinced in the course of your research that these two documents are to be found in the archives of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As somebody who worked in the supreme command, do you personally know -- were you aware that there was communication between the headquarters of the supreme command and the municipal headquarters in Konjic and the district staff in Zenica -- headquarters in Zenica -- about relocating the prison in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this particular case, it was the municipal headquarters of Konjic and they addressed the headquarters of the supreme command and asked that the prisoners from Celebici be transferred to Zenica, if possible. In this connection, the headquarters of the supreme command informed the municipal headquarters that it would be undertaking all measures to solve this problem, the problem to which the document of the supreme command refers. We have the district -- information from the district municipal headquarters of Konjic, whereby the supreme command refers to the Zenica district headquarters, in an attempt to try to solve the problem of relocating and transferring the prisoners from Celebici to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Brigadier, does all your research and your personal experience in your work with the supreme command, and your experiences as a professional soldier -- have they led you to a situation in which you are able to tell us whether, in the course of your research, you were able to come by the document whereby the prison of Celebici was established -- was formed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Regardless of my efforts to find this document, which I was interested in finding, I failed to find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of your research, Brigadier, did you manage to find a document appointing the warden of the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not come across such a document. I was interested in seeing who the warden was -- the commander was -- and whether he had the competencies and regulations for regulating matters in the prison. I did not find any document of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, in the course of your very intensive and conscientious report, did you come across any data or document by which Zejnil Delalic would be the individual who was the superior commander of the prison -- superior officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not come across any such document, on the basis of which I could maintain that Zejnil -- Mr. Delalic -- was the superior in the prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, I should now like to ask you to look at your document V-D/45. May we look at that document together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, who issued this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to the document, it was issued by the commission for the exchange of prisoners of war, and the contents of the document --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was the document signed -- is the document signed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Whose signature is on the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The President of the commission, Dzumhur Jasminka.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Has the document got a stamp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now to whom the document refers, this document on the exchange of prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It has to do with the municipal headquarters of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And what is the subject of the document, what does it pertain to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a request that prisoners be relocated -- transferred -- from Celebici to the sports hall, so that that section could be used for the purposes of the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, does this document contain all the formal characteristics which would to you, as somebody engaged in the study of this problem, would be a document upon which you could base your professional opinions -- is it a valid document in that sense?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a little difficult to say -- I am not an expert in legal matters -- I am not quite sure whether the document incorporates all the legal elements so as to make it binding and make it correspond to the intentions of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does it contain all the formal characteristics, that is to say, the signature, the stamp and the name of the organ issuing the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it customary that documents issued by a particular body be signed -- to be stamped and to be given a protocol number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this document has that particular form. It has the protocol, it has a signature and it has a stamp.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I should now like to ask you, Brigadier, to take a look at a document which the Prosecutor showed two days ago to the witness Mr. Hadzibegovic. It was the document, the State commission for the exchange of prisoners of war. I would like this document to be shown to the witness. I am not quite sure of the number of the document. Could you help me there, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecutor document 214. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I should like to ask you, Brigadier, to take a look at the document. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, in the course of your research, did you come across a document of this kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the first time that I have laid eyes on this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you: the document that was allegedly signed by the same person as the document we examined a moment ago, according to what is stated here, can you tell us when the document was drawn up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Without going into the contents of the document, I can give you my opinion. First of all, the document is not signed -- there is no stamp and, third, you can see that it was drafted on 22 December and it refers to the responsibilities of Tactical Group 1, which did not exist at that time, so, for me, this document is not a valid document -- it is unacceptable. It has three drawbacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I object, your Honour. Not more than about three questions back the witness said that he was not skilled in determining questions in relation to these particular types of documents and the criteria. He was then asked to recite whether there were stamps, signatures, et cetera, which he did. One can do that simply by reading the document. It speaks for itself. We do not need to hear that from evidence. Now he has moved on from a position where he says he cannot and is not qualified to comment on authenticity, to giving an opinion, and I object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The witness did not say more on that document -- after disclaiming --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours, I will not proceed on that document. Brigadier, we discussed a document which is evidence before the court dating back to 27 July, which shows Zejnil Delalic was nominated as commander of the Tactical Group for a given direction and, as far as we recall, you said that the document did not change the character of his function as the commander of Tactical Group 1. A moment ago, the Prosecutor sent us another document and, as I have enough copies of that document, I should like to tender it to the court and the witness so that I could ask my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think there may be a translation error -- because Madam Residovic said "a moment ago", it appears on the transcript as, "a moment ago" and I am sure she does not mean that because we certainly have not given her any documents this week, that I am aware of.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I made a mistake -- it was the 25th of last month when we received a portion of the documents from the Prosecutor. I think that is the document. Have you seen it? I ask that it be handed around. Have you looked at it, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It is a week ago, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I can confirm it was 25 March, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence document D146/1.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, would you look at the document? Brigadier, during your research, did you have an opportunity to see this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see this document for the first time now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether it is true that according to the document itself it was issued by the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is this document properly registered and dated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is this document stamped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, since by your interpretation of the appointment of 27 July and analysing all the documents that Zejnil Delalic as commander of the Tactical Group was issuing, you stated that he was the commander of the Tactical Group throughout this period, so on the basis of all this, does this document confirm this conclusion, or can you say something different to the Trial Chamber after reviewing this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I already said that I see this document for the first time, but it corroborates my view that he was never -- that Mr. Delalic -- and this was dated 8 August 1992, and it states that Mr. Delalic is commander of the Tactical Group in the area of Konjic and Jablanica and a certain Mr. Maric is also appointed here and here it clearly states that Mr. Delalic is not commander of all forces -- he is a commander of a Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Unlike the other documents which I have tendered, and given the relevance of this document, I tender it as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, it is admissible.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Brigadier, can you tell me whether, during 1992, you were personally acquainted with Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never met Mr. Zejnil Delalic. During the war I was on duty as a staff officer and I was -- and I had no opportunity to do so and I was in different parts of Bosnia during the war, but I never met him -- I was never in Konjic. In fact, I do not know who he is today in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have completed my questioning of this witness and we still have a matter to resolve. That is the tendering of the expert report. I know that you will make this decision at the end of the cross-examination. We would also like to offer the supporting material and my question to you is whether I should tender all these documents, including the report and the supporting material. I would like to tender the ones that were not compiled by this witness. Do you want me, in other words, to go from document to document and have the witness authenticate each one of these documents, or how would you want me to proceed on this matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think you tender documents which you think you can tender through this witness. If you have such documents, then at the end of the cross-examination, you might be able to do that. If you believe this witness can authenticate them and can claim any authority for their production, I think that if they pass through him, you may tender them. Otherwise, you may still rely on them for the purposes of his opinion. It might still be part of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Then, before completing my examination, I would just like to ask the witness whether he personally, through the director of the archives of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo, that is, in Konjic, established that the documents marked in his expert opinion under the following --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Before you do that, you have no difficulties with his report, because that is his own report produced by him. You can directly tender that. But when it comes to documents which he relies on for the purposes, it depends on the source of that report, because then who is entitled to tender them, or, if he created them himself, you might be able to tender them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My question to you right now was only whether to tender them now, or after the cross-examination. I thought that your suggestion was after the cross-examination. However, I could -- if I understood you correctly, I would be able to tender the report now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And, as far as my application for the tendering of the supporting materials are concerned, I will proceed in the same manner as I did with the witness Hadzibegovic testimony, that is, after the cross-examination. In that case, your Honours, I have concluded my examination-in-chief. May I just get the number of the last admitted document, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit D146/1.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Brigadier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any cross-examination by any Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vejzagic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Let me introduce myself. I am Zeljko Olujic and I represent Mr. Zdravko Mucic. You were examined by my learned colleague, Madam Residovic, and, in my examination, in the conversation that I would like to have with you, I would like to remind you what we said in the beginning; since we speak the language which we understand, I would just like you to wait until the question has been properly interpreted and so that everybody in the courtroom will be able to follow what we are discussing. Brigadier, you have very comprehensively answered a number of issues that were of interest in these proceedings. I would like to ask you several questions regarding the preparation for the war as you laid it out in your expert report -- the role of the JNA in Bosnia-Herzegovina and a few things about the situation in Konjic. May we start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you are talking about the preparation for the war by the JNA -- is that the issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Brigadier, that is how you prepared your report -- I am sorry for omitting that it was preparation for the war in SFRY. So, let me start off by asking you, who was the Minister of Defence of SFRY in those years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was Veljko Kadijevic -- he was the Federal Secretary. There was no special ministry, it was called the Federal Secretariat for People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: What was he by nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he was from a mixed -- he was of mixed origin. I think he was half Serbian, half Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: But he declared himself as a Serb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned military districts, was the Sarajevo military district dissolved accidentally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you had followed me correctly, armies were dissolved and the districts were established, and the intention was -- the goal was to pull the commands, the military commands, out of the influence of the republican leaderships, so that the republics would not have the influence over the army, and Slovenia especially objected to this when the Slovenian army was dissolved, and then after these armies were dissolved, the districts were established. So, the goal was, the objective was that the republican leaderships, since they had influence over the Territorial Defence, they feared that, if there were a crisis, that there would be a multi-Party system in the country, that Yugoslavia may break up, and they feared that these republican leaderships may influence the military top or the military leadership, and this is why these two districts were formed -- it was Belgrade and Nis and that was transferred to Skopje and the two new ones were established.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: What you are saying is there were very valid reasons for them to do so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, very much so, and then the Territorial Defence was also pretty much broken apart, because it was disarmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Brigadier. During your examination-in-chief, you also spoke of the military coup in March 1991, but do you know anything about the film about the arming of Croatia and about the attempted coup of January 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you are talking about the importing of weapons with Mr. Martin Spegelj; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Can that also be interpreted as an attempt at a coup?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Spegelj, being an experienced soldier -- he was a commander of the 5th Army Corps in Zagreb -- he knew what Belgrade was preparing. He knew what the intentions were, he saw that this might happen, that the Yugoslav People's Army would conduct an attack in order to relieve the leaderships of Slovenia and Croatia, and by a military coup, they may prevent the development of the democratic processes after the elections. They wanted to keep Yugoslavia by any means -- they were prepared to let go of Slovenia and Jovic said so in his book, that there was an agreement with certain republics to leave Yugoslavia and that there would be no obstacles there, and he was a member of the Presidency, who had taken the oath that he would defend the country. He is now betraying it -- he is saying that certain republics were offered to leave Yugoslavia, and that includes obviously Slovenia, which has a homogenous population and such agreement would not be offered to others. A Greater Serbia project was envisioned -- wherever there were any Serbs living, that was considered to be Serbian land. So, that was the Karlobag/Virovitica line. You have a map of Greater Serbia which was offered here, and it states, "Serbian brothers, this is your land. We have enclosed this." Only Zagreb would have been Croatian. There is no Dalmatia, and that was the policy of creating a Greater Serbia and Serbs were indoctrinated on this ideological basis, because it says, "Brother Serbs, these are your lands".

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And, also, there was also a saying, "Wherever there is a Serbian grave, that is a Serbian land"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, who was in command of the Territorial Defence? Was that in the competency of the republic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The role of the civilian authorities within the republic was such that they were to organise the Territorial Defence as an armed force. They were organising it, they were training it and equipping it, and also to pay the personnel, which had been transferred from the army to the Territorial Defence. However, republics and their institutions had absolutely no right to use the army. The general staff had a direct command and made decisions regarding Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Let me move to the role of the JNA in Bosnia-Herzegovina. In your expert report and in your testimony you talked about the relationship between the SDS and the JNA. Can we say that the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina had to take arms -- take up arms and fight against Bosnia, because otherwise they would be perceived as traitors by their fellow Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. The leadership of the SDS, with the assistance of Belgrade and the Orthodox church, for a long period of time indoctrinated the Serbian population through a number of events, telling the Serbian people that they were threatened, with the goal of creating a perception that this population was threatened, that the only way out for them was to stay in Yugoslavia, and they would discard everything else. In his report, the commander of the second military district, General Kukanjac -- and this is report number 908/1 -- he reports to the Chief of the General Staff, and General Blagoje Abzic was in the position at that time. He is reporting on the situation in Bosnia and he mentions the crisis and among other things he states that the position of the Serbian people is that the first and the only option is Yugoslavia -- they want to stay in Yugoslavia. The second option is a confederal Bosnia. We know what a confederation is, that is, a breaking-up of a statehood. A third option he says does not exist -- Serbs are ready to wage war -- it is obvious that they were prepared for war, because in that very same report he states that the 69,190 Serbian volunteers were armed in Bosnia as early as 20 March 1991 and this does not include the Territorial Defence and no member of these forces is in the army. So, there are almost 70,000 armed volunteers in Bosnia who are Serbs at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Brigadier. Can we say, based on all this, that the majority of Serbs in Bosnia, as well as in Croatia, were reserve forces of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not call it "reserve forces". The Serbs did not resist, they were not forced into it. For the most part, throughout 1991, in Croatia and Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina, those were parts of the 17th Tuzla Corps and the Banja Luka Corps, they took an active part in fighting in Croatia -- they were not forced into it. The Serbian Democratic Party, in collaboration with the command of the 17th Corps and the Banja Luka Corps, mobilised the Serbian population and the Bosnian Government objected to that, because they knew that they would go to fight their brethren Croats, and this is why the Minister of Defence, General Kadijevic, sent a very sharp warning to President Izetbegovic not to meddle in military affairs, and we know why the Bosnian Government took such a position, so the issue is that the Serbs were prepared, they were ready to go to fight, and you have the proof of that, that many of them were killed and, also, when the Maribor and Ljubljana Corps were retreating, they were first told to go back to Belgrade, and the 17th Corps suffered quite a few casualties and then they were asked to come and replace them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In Konjic, during the SFRY period, who was in charge there? Were Serbs in charge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know -- I did not research this. If you are asking me where the Serbs had a leading position?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had a leading position everywhere. I think that we need to clarify for the Trial Chamber, Serbs were saying that they were threatened, but even where they were in a minority, in Bosnia, they were only 32 per cent, they were in leading positions in all structures. For instance, in different ministries, in economic institutions, the key economic and industrial structures, communications -- they were not threatened. It is an allegation that was made up.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: You just mentioned ministries and industrial plants. How about the police and secret services, were they dominant there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Olujic, you are aware of that, that even in Croatia it was drastic, that the Serbian -- the Serbs only made 11 or 12 per cent there, and sometimes in the institutions, they were 60 to 70 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Brigadier. When you talked about the level of arms among Serbs in the Konjic area, when the Serbs were leaving villages, was that a signal that the JNA and the Chetniks would attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was obvious that there was propaganda and psychological pressure on the part of the SDS and the population needed to be pulled out so that people would not be killed in Konjic. This is what they did in Sarajevo as well, so if all Serbs would leave Konjic, then they could shell it, then they could attack it from the air, so that was first propaganda, initially. But the real objective was then to arm them, to create units of them, and then to prevent Serbs from being killed, because, if those towns were attacked, the Serbs may be killed by their own brethren.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: You talked about Serbs being armed in Bradina and Donje Selo. After they left these villages, did they continue to hide and were they still armed? Brigadier, you described well that people who surrendered arms were not touched. However, those who were found with weapons were disarmed. How about those who were hiding and were armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were such cases, and when the ground was searched, it was known that a lot of them have left their positions and some of them were hiding, and the police did searches. Some were found with weapons, some without weapons, and through different witnesses, their degree of responsibility was determined.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And did they wear uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some of them did, some of them did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Did they abide by the international rules of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: What I have in mind is when they were disarmed, according to what you know, were they abiding by the international military law? If you do not know --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. You mean whether the Serbian prisoners abided by the international military law?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, before they were arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, I meant after they were arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, before -- those who were armed, those who were hiding, those who were undertaking certain operations against the State, were they abiding by the international military law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: According to your knowledge, those who were detained and arrested, were they in a hierarchical-type of organisation, or was this a sort of an anarchic-type of resistance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to my research, in the area of Bradina, they had -- we heard that they had commanders, some Vojvodas, so there was some kind of organisation, but once they were broken up, I think that it was more anarchic after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. According to the laws of the former SFRY --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we might adjourn now, and resume at 2.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please kindly remind the witness he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, Sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand it, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
