utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Good afternoon, Brigadier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: We are almost at the end of my examination -- just several additional questions. Before the break, we started on an area which we interrupted. According to the SFRY laws, and the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, who had authority over prisons? Was this the Secretariat of Justice, later the Ministry of Justice, or was it someone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a legal question. I believe that it was the Ministry of Justice, and judicial organs -- I am not sure of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me whether the military, according to the law, could oversee the prisons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which prisons do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Civilian prisons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: How about Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: In those days, and when I say "in those days", I mean the period relevant to this indictment, did a whole range of different formations, some wearing uniform, some not, roam in the Konjic area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not in the Konjic area, so I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, I have no more questions for you. Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness. However, I have a request. We only received a very comprehensive amount of materials -- three volumes -- and I have not had an opportunity to review all the documents, so may I reserve the right to add potentially some additional questions for this witness on Monday? Again, I repeat that it is voluminous material -- to be honest with you, I was only able to review the first half, approximately, of the documents. Over the weekend I will try to attempt to review the rest of them, so should I have any additional questions that come from that second part of the documents, may I have your leave to ask several additional questions? I thank you in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That will be satisfactory, before the Prosecution starts. We might be able to accommodate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: May it please the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Moran.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Good afternoon, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Brigadier, I have a few questions I would like to ask you and some of them will be general questions and I am going to ask that the usher give you volume III of the documents, simply because I am going to use some documents in here just as examples of things, and then I will ask you a couple of specific questions and I think that that may be it -- at least I may be able to let you go home for the weekend or take the weekend off. The first thing I would like to chat with you about, Brigadier, is the law of command and the right to command and how command worked, both in the old JNA when you were an officer there, and then in the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as existed in the months immediately after independence, so May, June, July, that part of 1992. Now, you testified, I guess it was yesterday, that in any command and control system there has to be one commander who makes the decisions and is responsible for his unit; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That would be one of the principles of any military anywhere in the world, would it not, or at least any efficient military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is one of the principles, that is, command and control. It is called single command. I do not know how it is in other armies. I believe it has to be similar. A single commander issues commands and is responsible for his decisions so that means that a single commanding officer, so I do not know about the other armies, but we had it that way. There is one commander who is responsible for the use of his units. He can delegate his authority to his subordinates, but he cannot pass on the responsibility for what happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And in fact he can delegate as much or as little authority as he wants, can he not, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So I will bet some time in your military career you worked for a commander who would say, "Get this done" and he would let you do it anyway you wanted and I bet you also worked for a commander at some point in your military career who would tell you exactly how to do things, and not give you the freedom to choose; is that correct, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you delegate your authority to your subordinate in order to solve a problem, so within the framework of such a decision by the commander, the subordinate may carry out this task, but will not bear any responsibility for the consequences that may arise in the process of carrying out this task.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I guess what I was getting at was more along the lines of different commanders would have different styles, some commanders would allow their subordinates a lot of leeway in how to accomplish tasks and others would give them little tasks, or supervise them very carefully, and it is just a matter of the style that the commander has -- is that fair?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I did not hear the interpreter, so I am not sure when the question has been fully interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just start over. It might be a little bit easier. Different commanders that I worked for and I suspect different commanders that you worked for had different styles of the way they did things, so, for instance, a commander may just generally give a task to a subordinate, and a different commander, when he wanted the subordinate to do things, would be very specific in how he would tell them how to do it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And, one of the things, just to be upfront with everybody, we have talked several times -- there is no surprise that you and I have had conversations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And yesterday, when we were having a conversation, we talked about the right of someone who is not a commander -- the power of someone who is not a commander -- to give a binding order to another member of the military and the example that we talked about was someone who may be not a commander but is, say, a major in the army and would he have the right and the power to give a binding order to someone who was a lieutenant simply because of his rank, and you said, "No, he would not"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is no such right of command -- issuing commands to another. One cannot just meet someone and issue an order, because he is not his superior, so a subordinate only listens to and carries out the order of his own superior officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: When you say "superior", you mean someone who is in, if you would, the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the chain of command he can be -- for instance, if he is my superior, he has the right to issue orders to me. However, if I go somewhere and I am met by a general, say, and he tasks me with something, I do not have a duty to carry out a task given to me by him, even though he has the rank of a general, because he is not my superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay, thank you very much. Let me go on to a different subject. By the way I am going to say "general" at some point and I am going to promote you and I hope you do not mind -- and if I could arrange it, I would have you get the pension for a general rather than the pension for a brigadier. A commander, of course, cannot function alone -- he has deputies and he has staff members and other people that work for him and help him carry out his functions; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A commander of a district, let us say the second Sarajevo district, that is a very large command -- 400 strong, so it is a very large apparatus -- it has its structure, it has its assistants, it has its own headquarters. It is a fully developed command numbering 300 to 400 personnel, and, in the command structure, regardless of the size of the apparatus, the commander is the only one who has the authority to take decisions and only such commands -- those commands can be carried out or may be carried out. Let me elaborate. Let us say when a commander receives an order, let us say, in a state of war, he gathers his narrow circle -- that is, the group of deputies and he tries to find out how to carry out this task. He also has to be able to listen to his collaborators. Regardless of his experience, his training, his education, he cannot know all the arms, all the branches and he cannot know how to most efficiently use the forces that he has at his disposal. So, the engineers, the logistics, communications and so on, so he receives their input before he reaches his final decision. When he is satisfied that he has received all the information, then at one point he decides. He can adopt certain proposals or not, but he is responsible for the decisions that he has adopted -- not, let us say, a chief of artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And sometimes people who are subordinate to the commander, people who are on the staff, or maybe their adjutant will act for the commander, is that not true? I will give you an example of what I am talking about. If you look at document V-D/46, which is on the -- the Bosnian is on 831 and the English is on page 832 of volume III. I am just using this as an example. If you look at the signatures, the signature block down at the bottom, it has "Commandant, Army Bosnia-Herzegovina, Konjic," and a Major, followed by the Major's name. But if you look below it, the signature -- it looks like it is a different name, it looks like somebody else signed it for the commander? Do we have the same document -- it is an appointment --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That would be the kind of thing that would occur in your army or my army, I guess in any army, is it not, that it was not -- whoever it was who signed that, that was making these appointments, it was the commander who was making the appointments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My apologies, let me just find the signature. I see that it is a major, I see that it is a commander of the municipal headquarters in Konjic. I am not sure about his signature, so let me try to double-check it by comparing it with signatures on some other documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Actually the next thing I was going to ask you to do was look at document 50, which is a few pages back on page 843 in Bosnian. It is another appointment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have it paginated here. Can you please tell me again?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Document number D/50. It is about 20 pages behind -- go the other way -- 20 pages further on than the one you were just looking at.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So D -- which number, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You can see they appear to be the same commander, just that one is -- it appears that someone signed for one of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you can see two different signatures there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And that would be a reasonable thing to do if, for instance, this commander, whatever his name is -- how would you pronounce it -- Catic, Caric -- however you pronounce the Major's name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The name is also written differently -- it is Mirsad Catic and the other is Catic Mirsad. Maybe they are two different people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Would they be the same people or is it different person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is one person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He describes himself differently. One appears as the surname and then the first name and it is the opposite in the other document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the order is different.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: But it is in all likelihood the same person -- we are talking about the same rank, the same name, the order signed a few days apart and all I am getting at is that it would not be uncommon for a commander to make an appointment, as is made in document number 46, assigning several people to new duties, and have someone other than the commander sign for the commander to make the order official?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this specific case I see there are two signatures there, so that means they were not signed by the same person. I do not know where the commander Catic's signature is. That is not the right way of doing it. If somebody else was authorised to sign this document, it should have stated, "For the commander", so, where you have the line where it states "Commander", you say, "For the commander", if this person is authorised. I do not know -- in the previous document you can see that somebody else signed it. You see, I do not know the Commander Catic's original handwriting, so I cannot tell. So, you have to put in front of "Commander", "For the commander" and that means that this person was authorised to sign it on behalf of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is what I am getting at. I am just using these as examples and that someone, may be an adjutant, could sign an order for the commander, even though -- when in fact the commander had made the decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the commander can be on holiday, for example, for 30 days and then he writes the order and delegates somebody to represent him and to command the unit or anything else -- if the commander is absent for any longer period of time, then he designates somebody else to act in his -- on his behalf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Moran, if I understand you, you have not been against delegation of duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, all I am trying to get at is you can delegate duties but not responsibility and that people can sign for the commander, but it is within the parameters that the commander has -- has given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Your argument has always been one of delegation of responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Of course, the General has just testified that we can never delegate responsibility, just authority. For instance, General, a chief of staff or a deputy commander has no independent authority in his own right and all the authority he has to issue orders and to command people or to tell people what to do is based on the authority that is given to him by the commander; is that fair, general?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it would. The commander can authorise his helpers or deputies, or whoever, to, in given situations, perform tasks on the basis of his decision. However, the person to whom these authorisations have been delegated cannot be responsible for the outcome of a decision made by the commander -- it is always the commander who is responsible, and that is what I talked about when I spoke about "principles". It is one individual -- it is understood that one individual is always the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And, General, in the Bosnian army or the old JNA, did anyone other than a commander have the independent right to punish people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depends. It is regulated by the regulations governing the service. In addition to the units there were the departments led by the department heads, chiefs and they used their authority according to rank, so they were not in the army, but there were the different departments and the rank of a division commander, for example, if we are talking about a soldier, usually they did not have soldiers in these units, but they did use the right of rank. So the commander would be, for example, a colonel, and if he was head of a department, then he would use the rights vested in the colonel of such a unit -- the head of such a unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Let me come at it this way. The deputy commander, or the chief of staff of a unit, would he have the independent authority to punish members of that unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Usually he would not punish members of his unit. He could use his rights in the case when a commander -- given commands by the commander and he did not carry these out and so, on behalf of the commander he can do this, he can avail himself of this right given to him by the commander whom he represents at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Anything a non commander does, be it order people, carry out duties, punish people, whatever, is based completely on authority that is given to him by the commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Regardless of that person's rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He cannot use the right of a rank of the commander -- only if the commander is absent and he is performing the function of commander then he uses the same rights. For example, the commander of a division, if he has left on holiday, then his deputy will use the rights of the commander at that particular time, so he can punish the members just as if he were the division commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Because he is basically the acting commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: General, a few quick questions specifically on Celebici and if you do not know, "I do not know" is a fair answer. Do you know whether the staff of Celebici were members of the regular army of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time that is relevant to the indictment from May through August or September of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If that was the period, then, yes of course they were members of the regular forces, whether we are talking about the HVO or the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: But they were legally constituted by the sovereign Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not quite sure what you are talking about. I did not understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sure. The Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was a sovereign State, legally constituted the forces that provided the guards for the Celebici camp -- the staff for the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not up to the Government to decide about that particular staff. The Government has other competencies. We are dealing here with a case in point, a concrete case. It was a prison and the Government cannot determine the guards and staff of the camp. That is not something that is up to the Government to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I understand, General, that the supreme command in Sarajevo did not decide where every private was going to be assigned. What I was -- I guess I did not make my question as clear as it could have been -- these guards were either members of the TO or the HVO, and that those were legally constituted parts of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And where is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I was asking whether that is true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I have understood you correctly, your question refers to the staff that was determined to cater to the prisons, to the camp. In that case, the staff assigned to the camp -- it is not subject to the discipline from his superior. Let me give you an example of my battalion. In my battalion I was asked to give soldiers -- 10 soldiers in staff for the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I think I did not ask the question right. Let me try it again. That is not what I was getting at. Basically what I want to know is, you testified that these people were members, based on your research, that the staff of the Celebici prison were members either of the TO or the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning, the police as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Or the MUP, okay. Regardless of whether the TO -- these individuals were members of the TO or the MUP or the HVO, they were part of the legally constituted authorities and organs of the republic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. General. Your Honour, again, like Mr. Olujic and I think Mr. Niemann, I have been presented with more than a few documents, and with the court's leave, I would pass the witness now, but I would like to be able possibly to come back, whenever he comes back for cross-examination, and, prior to the start of the Prosecution's cross-examination, if there are any questions I have of the documents, I would like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You appear to be complicating the whole thing. You mean everyone passes the witness, waits for the Prosecution to cross-examine and then you come back?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No, heaven's no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: This is what you would appear to be doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: All I would ask, whenever the Prosecutor is going to cross-examine, if, before the start of the Prosecutor's cross-examination -- so I would go before the Prosecutor -- if there are some questions based on these documents, if I could ask those questions -- I do not think that the Prosecutor would have any objection to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: It is just a matter -- there is about 1,000 pages of documents here and every time I go through them, I find something I did not find the last time I went through them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I thought you did not have too many reasons to ask any questions, except you think you should.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I am afraid that if I go home this weekend and open up one of these books, I am going to sit there and see something I saw that I have not seen yet and wish I had asked about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is what life looks like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is true. But because we have had these for such a short time, I do not anticipate having any other questions, but I may -- depending on what is in this voluminous amount of documents, I may have something. Again, I do not think that the Prosecutor would object to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You need to some of your examination until after you have asked -- because, if the Prosecutor first indicated his inability to cross-examine, because of the volumes you have of them --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I have exactly the same problems that Mr. Niemann has and all I would ask is that I get the same -- rather than having to ask for a delay, I wanted to get what I thought was my cross-examination out of the way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You reserve the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, if it is okay with the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If it becomes necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: If it becomes necessary. That is fine. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any other cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, I have a very few questions. May it please the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Brigadier, my name is Cynthia McMurrey and I represent Esad Landzo. We had a short chance to visit at the early break this morning, did we not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And I want to discuss with you something on a different -- it has nothing to do with command structure of the Bosnian army or the JNA, but, basically, a tactic that may be used by all armed forces involving the use of young 18- and 19-year-old recruits. Can you tell me why it would be advantageous to utilise the young 18- and 19-year-old recruits, say, in the infantry and for the use in the armed forces? Can you describe the psychological makeup of these young men and why they are desirable to be in the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if I have understood you correctly, you are talking about soldiers who have just come for training, that is, to say, young recruits.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would be a crime to use young people of this kind in an armed struggle -- that is, those who have not mastered elementary military skills -- the use of weaponry, and conduct on the battlefield. What I want to say is that, in this war, too, although it was a very ghastly war, from the first days, we formed training centres and we did not allow these young recruits, these young men who had not had any military training, we did not allow them to go to the front, we did not send them to the front. Therefore, all those who were included in the fighting, without previous training, could easily have been subjected to injury or death, because they knew nothing about the principles of command, they did not have any essential knowledge of conduct on the battlefield, how to avoid artillery fire and shelling, and there was always the danger that young recruits of this kind would be killed, or wounded. This means that the recruits who were not trained and had not done their military service had to be prepared in some way through at least several months of training. In our programmes, this was usually between three and three and a half months -- the training programmes lasted that long so that they could master the elementary skills of warfare, to help the soldiers find their way around on the battlefield, because an untrained soldier, a recruit who knows nothing about the enemy, he will undergo great stress, because it is something that is unknown to him and every unknown factor leads to fear -- fear of the unknown. He does not know how to behave or indeed how he will behave, and, in situations of this kind, he might behave in quite an unnatural manner, especially if he has beside him a wounded colleague, or if somebody has died next to him -- what can happen is that he can just leave the battlefield and flee. He can be quite frustrated and undergo great shock and, as I say, a young recruit of this type should not be sent to the armed struggle.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: But at the time, in April and May of 1992, while you were forced to defend yourselves while being attacked by the Bosnian Serb forces, you did not have the luxury to send these young men to a three-month training camp, did you -- you had to use what was available at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the first days of the war, we formed centres, but many of these young recruits were not able to attend as members of units undergoing training, so there were those who, together with senior officers, were present and they had to grow accustomed to the battle front and to get experience and to know what a grenade means and that not every grenade means death. This was his sort of initiation. He had to adopt himself to the situation as he saw it on the battleground. There were cases in the war, in Sarajevo and in all parts of the battleground, where some of these young people, some of these brave and courageous young men quite simply could not restrain themselves and, if you give them weapons, they would be ready, they would show courage and advance like a lion and young men of this kind showed great courage at the beginning and many of them lost their lives through that bravery. We had cases where they would just march towards a tank. Can you imagine a young man with a rifle advancing towards a tank, because in fact he did not know what a tank meant? We had many misfortunes. We did not have the necessary professional cadres in the army and we were forced to send to command posts individuals who were not professionally trained. The army was not their profession. They did not have the elementary knowledge and skills necessary for officers. So, you would give him a company of 50 or 60 members, for example, and he had no idea of what to do with them, how to command them, how to line them up. He did not know how to organise the fighting, once he had received his orders and how to solve the problem that he had in hand and, for that reason, we organised a school, very early on, for the training of cadres. We had crash courses for our commanding officers so as to train them and equip them to be able to fight more successfully and to lead their units with as few casualties as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: In fact you can identify with what was happening in Konjic in 1992, even though you were not stationed in that area, because you were there in 1942, defending the same Konjic area basically under the same circumstances in the "Battle of the Wounded", is that not true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was a young man, too, in 1942. I knew nothing about warfare. I was given a rifle and my first -- I was given ammunition and we went to Tomislavgrad and we had five bullets. We were told not to shoot, to stay with our senior colleagues and to experience that night and to see what fighting looked like at night and in the Second World War we had no commanding officers to train us, but we had to gain our experience through practice and learn from our older members, who had joined the Partizan army previously. Of course, we also experienced fear and stress and we had to learn by trial and error, in practice, during the combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, you testified yesterday that one of the main problems of this outbreak was that you had no weapons, you had no ammunition, but most of all you did not have any trained officers to take command in the lower echelons of the forces in the Konjic area, so to summarise what you testified just a while ago, what you were saying was that, because you did not have people who had leadership training, you did not have people who had been formally trained in the JNA as officers; these people that were formerly electricians and mechanics were now in the position of leadership of a deputy commander and that kind of title, and they did not have any training in order even to train these young recruits with no military training, so it was the blind leading the blind, basically?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, the situation was similar to the one you have just described. Practice, life, the war, made us use fighters who had shown courage and an elementary sense of organisation -- they were selected to be officers, whereas they might have been electricians or mechanics or whatever, so he was given a company to command, or a platoon or whatever. This, of course, was not a good thing, but it was born of necessity -- we had no choice in the matter, and in the initial fighting, in the initial operations, we had a lot of problems. We had more dead and wounded than we had trained professional officers, who knew something about warfare.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I want to ask you about possibly the lowest ranking soldier on the totem pole which would be possibly a prison guard, and when a prison guard is assigned to a barracks, does he have any authority to change the structure or the command or the conditions of the barracks that he is in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand your question fully, but I think I know what you want to ask me. The lowest echelon in the army was the rank of private -- a private first-class, whereas the others were the non-commissioned officers, so these privates could only have the duty of replacing the guards, which means that a facility, say, had perhaps 10 guards in position, which means 10 guards in one shift, 10 guards in another shift and so on, and this would form a guard of some 30 guards. So that would be the unit, the guard post, and the private, if it is winter, he would bring in new guards every hour or every two hours. He has no other authorisation -- just to see that the guard system was rotated and that the guards replaced each other after a set amount of time. He had no other authorisation or competencies. I do not know whether that answers your question. I do not know if I understood you correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I think it answered all my questions. I want to say your testimony has been most interesting and instructive and I really thank you very much. I pass the witness, your Honour. I do not need any time to go through any volumes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Niemann, will you start your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I would like to renew the application that I made at the beginning of the week in relation to the cross-examination of this witness. My position is -- I have been in court all week and have been dealing with the other witness and the material in relation to that witness. I would ask that the cross-examination by the Prosecution be put off until the close of the other witnesses, which were scheduled, or Thursday, whichever comes first. I believe, your Honour, it would be a much more efficient way of dealing with it, because I can consider that if I have more time to prepare, I will be able to reduce the amount of cross-examination rather than extend it. Your Honours, I understand there are other witnesses ready and waiting to come into court. There would be no loss of time as far as the court is concerned. It is my application that when confronted with all this material, it really needs to be studied in detail and I wish to do that before I embark upon cross-examination and, as I say, we only received it a day and a half working days before court started this week, which is on Thursday afternoon, so we really have not had the time -- I have not had the time that I would need to devote to it, to effectively devote to it. So that is my application, your Honour, that, if we can proceed with the other witnesses that are available and ready to testify, then Thursday would be a good day to complete all the cross-examination and I would certainly complete it in that time and leave sufficient time for some other questions from counsel, should they arise, and any re-examination on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Niemann. Ms. Residovic, can you proceed with your next witness, if possible, now so --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, have I heard your decision yet, given that this witness has been examined and cross-examined for quite a while, and his overall condition is such that it would be better if he came back on Monday, and, as I was not aware of how long my colleagues would be cross-examining, I have not called my next witness until 4 o'clock, so the next witness would be ready at 4. I would also request that the witness Vejzagic be brought back Monday to be cross-examined by the Prosecution and any other cross-examination by my colleagues, so as for the other witness, I called him at 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If you would prefer to come back at 4 for the next witness, if we are able to finish with this witness by Monday, I suppose we might be able to take the cross-examination then. That would be a good arrangement. We will rise now and come back at 4pm.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Before the witness comes in, I just wish to raise again the matter that I raised beforehand, because I was not sure what our position was in this. My position was, your Honour, at the beginning of the week, that I really do feel that I will not be in a position until the end of the first three witnesses and, if they are finished on Monday, by all means I will be ready to start my cross-examination, but I would think that is unlikely so that would make it Thursday, bearing in mind there are two days off next week. I re-emphasise the fact that we were given this vast amount of material at the eleventh hour, which really did preclude us from being in a position to prepare. I might just go on and say we have now been given another bundle of material, five minutes ago, literally, in relation to the next witness. Your Honour, it is impossible to prepare a proper cross-examination of a witness in circumstances where we are given material this late. Goodness knows how long Madam Residovic has had this material, but it makes really quite a mockery of the provisions in the Rules which talk about reciprocal discovery and bearing in mind all the things they have said about us during the course of the Prosecution case and never we were so egregious as to present this amount of substance at this sort of late hour, so we do protest. And I am not at all sympathetic to a situation where Madam Residovic says, "Well, the old gentleman has been here for a long time. Monday morning he should be able to finish his evidence." Madam Residovic should have thought of that well in advance of discovering so late that no party could be in a position to be prepared. Really, it does make the case so much more difficult if this sort of procedure is allowed to continue time and time again in relation to the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, after the last comments by my learned colleague Niemann, which I believe are not merited, I think that it would be appropriate for you to advise Mr. Niemann not to address me in this manner. I think that we need some basic decency here and talking about matters of principle, as far as the obligations of the Defence counsel are concerned, I have already stated that I have immediately turned over the documents that we received and, if the Prosecutor's Office checked their files, they will see that they have more files than they have ever received from any international organisations. If the Defence had received the documents five days ago and sent it for translation and have received it back today at 12 o'clock, then we have completely abided by our obligations and I do not appreciate the comments being made about me. I am not saying that we have never received anything in a timely way by the Prosecution, but sometimes we would be given some directly here at the bar, and I would just one more time like to point out we need to have some kind of equity here. We do not have all the arms, we do not have all the available resources that they do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I would have thought the problem should be over by now. You have been together for quite some time. If there is any misunderstanding, one could have ameliorated it with smiles and jokes instead of getting so cross and bitter about it. I know occasionally these things do happen. One supplies certain things late, but I think you can still carry on despite such a late service of some of these things. You might as well call your witness and let us carry on and see how far we go. (The witness entered court).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. SENAD BEGTASOVIC

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Even though you know me, I am going to introduce myself. I am Edina Residovic, Defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic. Sir, would you please introduce yourself to the Trial Chamber by stating your full first and last names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Senad Begtasovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, before I ask any questions of you, I am going to ask you to just let me give you a technical advice. You and I speak and understand the same language. However, the things that you and -- what you and I talk about, the others can only receive through the interpreters, who have a very responsible and difficult task. So, I would like to ask you, whenever I pose a question, please do not answer it immediately. You have a headset on the desk next to you. Please listen there until the interpretation is complete and only then proceed with your answer. It is the only way in which everybody will be able to follow. Did you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understood that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Begtasovic. Mr. Begtasovic, when were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born on 1 January 1952.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where were you born, Mr. Begtasovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in Konjic, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where do you live, Mr. Begtasovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I live in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What is your citizenship, Mr. Begtasovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is -- I am a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What are you by profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: An attorney.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What is your education?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I graduated from the law school in Sarajevo in 1975.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After graduation from law school, did you take special exams which are a requirement for acting as a judge and as an attorney at law by the laws of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is a bar exam which is a requirement for working as a judge or prosecutor or a lawyer and I passed it in 1976.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before becoming an attorney at law, which is your current position, did you also work in any of the positions for which you had qualified by taking the bar exam?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, between 1976 and 1995, I was a judge at the basic court in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since when are you an attorney at law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since 1 February 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, as a judge, and as a lawyer, were you involved in criminal cases?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, could you tell the Trial Chamber where were you in early 1992, more specifically in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In April 1992 I was in Konjic and I held the post of the president of the court in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, do you know when Bosnia-Herzegovina proclaimed its independence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After the declaration of independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina on 6 April 1992, did the war start immediately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, with the exception of your years when you studied in Sarajevo, did you spend your entire life in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In terms of ethnic groups, who lived in Konjic and who continues to live in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Konjic was a typical multi-ethnic Bosnia-Herzegovinian town. Bosniaks, Serbs, Croats, Jews, some Hungarians, some Czechs and some gypsies lived there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What were inter-ethnic relations before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were very harmonious. Very few people in my town considered the ethnic background as something that sort of gives them a dominant stamp. Mixed marriages were very frequent. I come from a mixed marriage -- I am sorry, I am married to a Serb woman and my children come from a mixed marriage.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Even though the ethnic background was not very important, did we still know before the war, and did we take care that in different institutions in the local government members of all ethnic groups were to be represented?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was the official policy.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you worked in the court, Mr. Begtasovic, can you tell me whether the composition of the court also reflected the ethnic -- the distribution of different ethnic groups in town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the eve of the war, there were 10 judges in the court in Konjic. Three judges were of Serbian background, three of Croatian background, and four, including myself as the president of the court, were of Bosniak background.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you were a judge and later the president of the court in Konjic. Can you please tell me, what kind of a court was it, in other words, what are the competencies of this court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The primary court, besides the civil cases that it tries, also tries criminal cases which envisage the sentences for up to 10 years. For criminal cases which give a higher sentence, the authority is in the court in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me under whose jurisdiction was the establishment of courts in our republic in those days, according to the law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the competence of the republican authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who was appointing the judges of your court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the republican assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did the laws about the establishment of courts and the appointment of judges change up until the Dayton Accords in 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, they did not change.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, as a citizen of Konjic, you can surely -- you will surely be able to answer the following question: were you in Konjic in April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did there come a time in April 1992 when Konjic was surrounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Konjic was surrounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what it means to you that it was a surrounded town -- what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the south-east there is a village of Borci -- in the surroundings of which there were SDS paramilitary formations. The highway leading to Sarajevo was cut off at the village of Bradina, so that the communication line between Konjic and Sarajevo was cut off. The highway leading to Mostar was also blocked, because, in the area of Donje Selo, which is the area that controls the M17 highway, and from this area this road to Mostar can be very effectively controlled, so the town was surrounded in the sense that you could not go either to Sarajevo or to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, do you know whether patients, that is, sick people, were unable to leave Konjic after the second half or the latter half of April 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nobody could leave Konjic, including the sick people.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, how did the citizens of Konjic respond to the beginning of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina and to the developments in Sarajevo and to this surrounding of their own town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can say that, at first, a panic struck. None of us, like any other Europeans, had any experience of shelling of a town -- the dangers of walking in the street and the beginning of a great hunger.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, let me ask you some questions that are closer to your professional concerns. We have heard on issues that we have discovered from some other witnesses. Apart from the primary court, which was in Konjic before the war, was there a military court in Konjic at any time before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, until the war there was no military court. Such a court was in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If, in the area of Konjic, a serious crime were committed which was under the competence of your court, where would such a crime be investigated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The investigation of such a crime would be conducted in the higher court in Mostar, or in the military court in Sarajevo, if such a crime was within the competence of that court.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was there a prison in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where would persons who committed serious crimes be detained -- such persons that should have been detained in a prison during the investigation period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Such persons would be detained in the district prison in Mostar and in the correction centre in Zenica and (INAUDIBLE).

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, was there in Konjic anybody that could change the competencies of your court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because the change of competencies of our court was a part of the authority of the Parliament.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, does this refer to both the real and the local competence of your court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are correct -- to both.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that at the beginning of the war on 6 April 1992 you were the president of the court. Mr. Begtasovic, was there a period of time after the beginning of the war in Konjic when your court was not working?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Practically speaking, the court in Konjic did not function throughout 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us some of the reasons for this situation in the municipal court in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Practically a daily shelling of the town of Konjic prevented reporting to duty -- not only of the personnel of the court, but also arrival of witnesses, parties in lawsuits -- all participants.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, did a certain number of judges from your court leave Konjic at the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How many judges were there to try criminal cases?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was the only one.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Criminal court judge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mean you stayed in Konjic -- you were the only one who remained in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean, Mr. Begtasovic, that throughout 1992 your court was not able to function, even for the types of crimes for which it was there to try?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago you told me that, in Konjic, there was no prison and that individuals who, in the Konjic locality, had committed crimes were taken to the prison of the district court in Mostar. Tell me, please, Mr. Begtasovic, do you know, according to our regulations, who had the authority over those prisons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Ministry of Internal Affairs of Bosnia-Herzegovina was the authority for the prisons there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were these prisons under the authority of the Ministry of Justice, and general management? Can I hear your answer, because by nodding your head we will not be able to translate you, so please put it in words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you are right, it was under the competence of the Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you were a witness to all these events and that you were a professional and had knowledge of these events, please tell me whether, in the course of 1992, whether throughout 1992 conditions existed for transferring detainees from Konjic to Mostar or Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In explaining the town's encirclement I mentioned the approach to Mostar from Konjic was not possible and you were not able to approach Sarajevo from Konjic, either. In that way, it was impossible to take the detainees -- people who were believed to have committed a crime, to these prisons -- the prisons that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was this impossibility directly linked to the war operations in the area -- in those areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that it was not possible to transfer the prisoners to Mostar and Sarajevo. I think that the circumstances through other evidence are well known to us. Please tell us now whether there was the possibility of transferring the prisoners to other areas, and I have in mind here both legal possibilities and actual possibilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was no such possibility whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, whether there were attempts to change the competencies and to have prisoners from Konjic in the autumn of 1992 transferred to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know whether it was in the autumn of 1992, but I do recall there were attempts of that kind. At one time, I had contacts with General Divjak and Kukanjac. When that was exactly I am not sure, but in my conversations with them I learnt there were attempts to change the competencies, that is to say, to create a military court for the Konjic locality.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, were there any regulations which enabled the creation of a military court in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1992, there were no regulations of this kind -- no possibilities of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when the legal prerequisites emerged for a military court to start functioning in Konjic -- a department of the military court to begin operations in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A department of the district military court in Mostar, which was located in Konjic, started functioning as far as I remember in the autumn of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, was that the earliest possible time to bring before a court in Konjic criminal investigations for individuals who had committed crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, in view of the fact that there were no courts, tell me, please, if there was any doubt that somebody had committed a serious crime, does the absence of a court -- did the absence of a court mean that these people were not taken to prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would be impermissible to propagate an attitude of this kind. If a crime has been committed, the perpetrator must be taken prisoner, regardless of whether a court exists -- arrested -- a court that would bring him to justice.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Which organs in Konjic were authorised organs to perform arrests -- who were these organs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were members of the Internal Affairs Ministry, quite definitely and the military police, later on, of the Territorial Defence, the TO -- the military police of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, when you look back to those days, did you as a citizen of Konjic and as a judge yourself in Konjic, in the summer of 1992, think that the war would end very quickly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We all thought that the war would not last until the autumn.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you expect anybody's aid and assistance? Did you think that somebody else should help a country attacked in that way and a member of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we just could not encompass anything of that kind, that is, that at the end of the 20th century in the heart of Europe -- and Bosnia is the heart of Europe -- that a war could be waged and that somebody could shell towns, just like that. We thought that this was absolutely impossible.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you consider it normal for the world to stop a war of this kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, Mr. Begtasovic, I am sure you did not wait in Konjic, but do you know whether the competent authorities in Konjic reacted to this state of affairs in April 1992 and did they take the necessary steps for Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was a general mobilisation of the citizens proclaimed in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, general mobilisation was proclaimed in April -- I think it was around 20 April.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did all the citizens -- were all the citizens of Konjic duty bound to respond to the call for a general mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, or to go to their working duties, or as members of the Civil Defence units, or as members of the army, that is, it was the Territorial Defence at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If anybody failed to respond to this call for mobilisation, did this represent a criminal act according to our laws?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was considered a criminal act.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did a substantial number of the Serb ethnicity, your co-citizens, fail to respond to this call for mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would be correct to say that a very small number of the Serb ethnicity joined in the general call for mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Begtasovic, which forces, after April 1992, considered themselves to be the defence forces of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were the units of Territorial Defence and, later on, as of June 1992, they were the units of the Croatian Defence Council, because the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, according to a law enacted in May pertaining to the armed forces, were made up of the units of Territorial Defence and the HVO units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The units of the internal affairs units, were they a component part of the defence forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you are right, and the units of the Internal Affairs Ministry.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether, apart from these defence forces in Konjic in that period, any other paramilitary units existed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard of the existence of similar paramilitary units, which were organised by the SDS, but I do not know any particulars, because I was not personally informed of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, as a citizen of Konjic, did you hear that there were some private armies in Konjic, in existence in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Apart from the SDS units, I did not hear of any other units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, do you know whether, in the course of May, in order to lift the siege of the town, that is, in May 1992, some combat operations took place -- did these combat operations take place to lift the blockade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard about this, but I was not acquainted with any of these military operations. At that time, I was outside the realm of these matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Begtasovic, that the town of Konjic -- that it was not only encircled, surrounded, but that it was intensively shelled -- began to be shelled intensively?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the beginnings of May 1992, grenades fell on Konjic daily.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Begtasovic, whether, from the surrounding villages, the population was expelled and, if it was, could you tell us who expelled the population and which population was expelled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that near Boracko, the lake of Boracko, the Bosnian population was expelled from the village of Gakici. I know that, from Bijela, the Bosnian and Croatian population were expelled, and some Bosnians from the Donje Selo area and Bradina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me please whether at that period, in May 1992, essential means for livelihood were lacking in Konjic -- were supplies lacking, were there general shortages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because all the shops from April 1992 were closed, and the population could gain supplies only in the Mehmamet, in Caritas and other organisations of this kind -- charity organisations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when the first convoy of the UNHCR came to Konjic with certain quantities of flour and other food supplies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was either in August or September 1992 -- I cannot quite recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, you said that you heard about certain combat operations for lifting the siege of Konjic, but I would like to ask you something else now. Did you, as a citizen of Konjic and as a judge, ever hear that, after these combat operations, a number of individuals were arrested and detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did hear about this, but not with enough, sufficient detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Then I do not think you will be able to answer my next question with any precision, but I am going to ask it anyway. Tell me, please, as far as you know with the details that you recall, some individuals were arrested on suspicion of having committed crimes, where they were placed, where they were taken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I know that some of these individuals were sent to Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who performed these arrests -- who detained these suspects?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, Mr. Begtasovic, in 1992 -- were you ever in the barracks or prison of Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, Mr. Begtasovic, have any knowledge of these individuals, these suspects, and the proceedings brought against them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During which time -- when?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After they had been detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, did you have any knowledge of whether a commission was set up to investigate the responsibility of these suspects?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the end of 1992, or perhaps the beginning of 1993, the municipal headquarters of the army set up a military investigating committee to investigate and it investigated over 100 cases, over 100 suspects who, at the time, were in the sports hall in Musala in Konjic. These individuals, these detainees, as far as I recall, were held in Celebici previously. I was a member of that military investigating committee, and I repeat, it was set up by the municipal headquarters of the army following orders by the commander of the 4th Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to ask if we may show the witness evidence D7/1. (Handed). . Mr. Begtasovic, would you please look at the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Do you have copies for us?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this present moment, I do not have any copies, because I thought that I was using evidence from the evidence and documents you already have, but we can supply you with a copy. I will copy the evidence every time, but I think this is evidence that has already been accepted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It has not been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Then I apologise, I thought that it had been admitted. Then I should like this document to be withdrawn, although I did think that it had been admitted. I am going to show it to the witness later on, when I have the possibility of presenting you all with a copy and its translation, because the translation of the document exists and we did submit it to the court. So I am going to carry on my examination of the witness, until we are all able to have a copy of this document before us. Mr. Begtasovic, as you said earlier on, at the end of 1992 or the beginning of 1993, you became a member of the committee. What was the task of that committee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The basic task of the committee was to investigate over 100 cases, that is to say, individuals who had been detained and who were suspects. They had been suspected of committing serious crimes of armed rebellion.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, did you personally hear these suspects?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a five-member committee, if I recall correctly, and, if I remember, I heard these individuals for the most part. Perhaps a number of -- some of the 100 were heard by another member of the committee, but, at all events, I did most of the hearing. I looked into most of the cases in the presence of all the other members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you make records of this hearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all the individuals I questioned, records and minutes were taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were these proceedings -- did these proceedings follow the letter of the law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the individuals were questioned according to regulations governing criminal procedure which was positive at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of your work within the committee, did you have occasion to see the previous dossiers, files, on these individuals -- the individuals that you yourself questioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was acquainted with their files. They were questioned by a committee which questioned them before my particular committee, and I did have occasion to see the files, although I did not devote any great attention to the files.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, Mr. Begtasovic, whether these hearings, these previous hearings, whether they were hearings which were performed by individuals whom you yourself personally knew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. For instance, I remember a colleague and a friend of mine, Goran Lokas. I recall the name of Miroslav Stenek. I recall the last name, that is, Mladen, Zovko, and right now those are the only names that I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: While questioning individuals, those 105, or however many persons were there, were you making regular records of their questioning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were these records signed by the members of the commission, that is, the individuals who were in charge of questioning these individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They should have been signed by them and I believe they were signed by them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were these records also signed by the persons who were questioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can I ask the usher's assistance to show the witness a certain number of records of questioning of suspects and I have sufficient copies for everybody in court and I have already provided copies for the Prosecution. May I have each of these records marked individually and then I will ask the witness to identify each one of them as a record of his individual questioning of each of these individuals. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is a record.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please wait so the judges may receive their copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: May I ask that the Registrar may give us the numbers of every single one of these records so that I can put my number on every single record. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Every single record will have a separate number. The record of 9 January 1993 is Defence Exhibit D147/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon -- you should state the names of the interviewed persons, because many records are of the same date.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The witness can tell you the name, because I do not have my copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, could you tell us the record of whose suspect's interview is this, so that the Prosecutor is able to follow what we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the record of the interview with the suspect Dusko Bendzo, that is Dusko Bendzo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, will you please tell me whether, in the heading of this record, there is a name of the body whose member you were, and which was authorised to conduct the questioning of these individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It is the Military Investigating Commission of the 4th Corps and it is dated 9 January 1993 regarding the questioning of Dusko Bendzo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please turn to the page with the signatures and can you tell me whether you recognise the signatures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recognise my own signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So, you can confirm before this Trial Chamber that this is a record that you personally signed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since the witness has recognised and identified the document which he himself has helped compile and he has signed, I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have to object for the time being, at least, because we did not have any time to study these documents, so we kindly request that the question of the admissibility be postponed after cross-examination so that the Prosecution may study the documents, which arrived on this desk only at 5 minutes to 4, so that we can decide our position, whether to object or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What is the basis of your objection -- because you have not studied the document, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: We did not study the documents and, for instance, we might not object to the fact that this is a document signed by the witness, but we might object depending upon the specific contents of every single record. So, I would kindly request to postpone --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not think these are sufficient reasons for objecting to it, because he is one of the parties to this document. He is entitled to put it in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: In our opinion, a document like this is not admissible simply because it was signed by this witness. There are others --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If there are any disqualifying elements, let us hear them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact we do not know whether we can find any disqualifying element. It depends upon the contents of every single statement, which we have to be in a position to read before deciding our position. This is an investigator who signed a witness statement, so there is some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Even if you read it, what objection could you have? This is a record prepared by one of the persons who recorded the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would just like to add that, during the proceedings, we attempted to show to the representatives of the Prosecution similar records, and we were advised by the court to try to bring a witness who had actually questioned these suspects. So, I see no problem in all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You can indicate you have objected to it, but we will admit it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: If we do not know exactly the contents -- we know there were some witnesses of the Prosecution who say that many of -- well, some of these statements were taken under duress. We have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You can cross-examine them in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: If we cannot examine these records, we cannot know whether any of these records --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I agree with you but we will admit it on the caveat that you objected to its admissibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Can the witness please be shown the next record? (Handed). Can you please give me the number of the record which you have just given to the witness and --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The statement of Vukalo Risto made on 15 January 1993, Defence Exhibit D148/1.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can I have copies of this record to be passed on to the judges so that I may proceed with the questioning. Mr. Begtasovic, is this a record of the commission in whose work you participated during the questioning of this individual?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a record of an interview of the Military Investigating Commission of the 4th Corps on 15 January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is the record signed by members of the investigating commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is signed and I recognise my own signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where is your signature?
